problem: Earlier instruction-following agents had three gaps. Many worked in 2D grids or discretized worlds (Misra et al. 2017, Yu et al. 2017, Oh et al. 2017). Others used hand-crafted visual features or prior linguistic knowledge (Mei et al. 2015 used bag-of-visual-words, Oh et al. used an analogy objective). Most fused language and vision by simple concatenation, which does not ground object attributes (color, size, type) well from raw pixels in partially observable 3D worlds with continuous agent positions.
motivation: Task-oriented language grounding requires an agent to recognize objects in raw pixels, explore when targets are occluded or out of view, ground each instruction concept, and reason about pragmatics such as superlatives. Its policy must also generalize to unseen maps and unseen attribute-object combinations. The authors observe that trained conv feature maps tend to detect object attributes. An instruction should therefore select (gate) which feature maps matter rather than just being appended to them.
key_idea: Fuse the instruction with the image by passing the GRU instruction embedding through a sigmoid FC layer. This gives a per-channel attention vector that multiplicatively gates the CNN feature maps (Gated-Attention). The fused map is fed to an RL (A3C) or IL (BC/DAgger) policy trained end-to-end from raw pixels.
insight: Channel-wise multiplicative gating works as an attribute selector. The instruction switches on feature maps that respond to 'green', 'pillar' or 'short', which generalizes compositionally to unseen attribute-object pairs. In Table 1, swapping concatenation for GA (with slightly fewer parameters: 3.39M vs 3.44M for A3C) lifts A3C in the Hard mode from 0.24 to 0.83 on MT and from 0.12 to 0.73 on ZSL, so the gain is not from capacity. The attention-vector heatmaps show dedicated dimensions for armor (dim 18), skullkey (dim 8) and pillar (dim 36), and no dedicated type dimension for the generic word 'object'. t-SNE clusters by color, type and size, including for held-out test instructions. A second lesson is that imitation learning (BC/DAgger) collapses in Medium and Hard modes where exploration is needed, while A3C with an LSTM stays robust.
method: CNN image encoder: 3 conv layers (128 filters 8x8 stride 4, 64 filters 4x4 stride 2, 64 filters 4x4 stride 2, ReLU), adapted from the Arnold Doom agent, applied to a 3x300x168 RGB first-person frame to give x_I in R^{d x H x W}.
GRU instruction encoder: word sequence encoded by a GRU of size 256 into x_L; no pretrained embeddings or linguistic priors.

Gated-Attention fusion: a_L = sigmoid(FC(x_L)) in R^d (d = number of conv channels, 64). Each element is broadcast over HxW and multiplied element-wise (Hadamard) with x_I. Concatenation of the flattened vec(x_I) and vec(x_L) is the baseline fusion.

RL policy (A3C): FC 256, then LSTM 256 for memory of objects seen earlier, then a shared trunk with a value head (1 unit) and a policy head (3 actions). Trained with entropy regularization, GAE, SGD lr 0.001, discount 0.99, 16 threads. Reward is positive for reaching the correct object and negative for a wrong one, with no distance-based shaping.

IL policy (BC / DAgger): FC 512 into 3-way policy output, trained online with Huber loss against an oracle action (RMSProp, 10 epochs per iteration). The oracle uses engine-provided agent and target poses and turns toward the target, then moves forward. DAgger mixes oracle and learned policy with a linearly decaying coefficient.

ViZDoom grounding environment: 70 templated 'Go to the X' instructions over attributes (color, size, superlatives) and object types (torch, pillar, keycard, skullkey, armor). Each episode has 5 objects (1 correct, 4 distractors). Three difficulty modes: Easy (fixed agent, objects on a line), Medium (random objects within view), Hard (random agent and objects, exploration needed). Maximum episode length T=30.

setting.backbone: 3-layer CNN + GRU(256) with Gated-Attention fusion; A3C LSTM policy or BC/DAgger FC policy (all trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Procedurally generated ViZDoom episodes using 55 training instructions (15 of 70 held out) with random object combinations and placements. RL uses sparse success/failure reward; IL uses actions from an engine-state oracle.
setting.simulator: ViZDoom (custom Doom-based grounding environment introduced by the paper)
setting.privileged: none at test time (the oracle uses GT agent/target poses from the engine, but only for IL training supervision)

numbers_note: Table 1 prints accuracy as fractions (e.g. 0.83); these are converted to 0-100 SR here. Split mapping is my convention, not the paper's: MT (training instructions, unseen maps) is recorded as 'test' and ZSL (15 held-out instructions, unseen maps) as 'test-unseen'. Training curves for A3C (Fig. 5) appear only as figures.
results: On the new ViZDoom benchmark, A3C with Gated-Attention is the strongest model. It reaches 1.00/0.81 (Easy), 0.89/0.75 (Medium) and 0.83/0.73 (Hard) accuracy on MT/ZSL. The strongest baseline, A3C-Concat (an adapted Misra et al. 2017), gets 1.00/0.80, 0.80/0.54 and 0.24/0.12, so the gap grows with difficulty. GA also beats concatenation under imitation learning; for example, DAgger GA vs DAgger Concat on Medium is 0.55/0.40 vs 0.45/0.23. However, IL methods degrade sharply in Medium and Hard modes (≤0.55) because they do not explore.
limitations: Toy setting: 70 templated 'Go to the X' instructions, 5 objects per episode, simple Doom maps and 30-step episodes. There is no free-form language or realistic 3D scenes.
Evaluation uses only 100 episodes per cell with no variance or seed reporting, and accuracy is the only metric (no path efficiency).
Imitation-learning variants rely on an oracle with engine-provided poses and perform poorly when exploration is required. The only fusion baseline is concatenation.
